title: The First Ringing
subtitle: Friday 10 to Thursday 16 October 1924: A Bell in a Crate, Three Claims and No Bodies, a Seance on the Shore Road, and the Bottom of the Tide

setting.name: Carrow Island, the week of the full moon, October 1924
setting.description: The party arrive on the mail boat on Friday 10 October with the recast church bell in the hold and five days before the next spring low water. The island is quiet, polite, and shut: three people have walked into the sea since August, a fourth is said to have, and the islanders have stopped talking about it to anyone from away. The moon is full on Monday 13 October; the lowest night low water of this spring tide is Tuesday 14 October at 6:21 p.m., an hour and a half after dark, and the drowned bell will ring then whether or not anyone is ready. The scenario asks the party to learn, in five days, three of the bell's rules: when it rings, whom it calls, and how it can be answered, and to save the life of whoever it calls. Everything they need is on the island, in a lighthouse logbook, a sexton's ringing book, a minister's bequest, a widow's sugar tin, a ballad, a burying ground, and the memory of a seventy-three-year-old woman who will not see them.
setting.atmosphere: Fog for the first two days, so thick that the Harbor's houses vanish twenty yards up the hill and the Head's fog bell strikes all night; then a hard bright northwest wind on Sunday that blows it away and shows the whole bay blue and white to the mainland hills. Short days, early dark, frost on the wharf planks at dawn. The island goes on: lobster boats going out at four, women hanging washing, men splitting wood, the Grange supper on Saturday, a memorial service with no coffin on Sunday. But every door has iron over it, nobody goes down to the Bar after dark, and on Tuesday afternoon, as the light goes, the Harbor families go indoors one by one, lock up, light lamps, and sit up together in their kitchens to wait. Dread before horror: in this scenario nothing attacks anyone. The bell rings, a person walks, and the party have to stop them.

keyLocations.name: Carrow Harbor: the wharf, the Proprietors' Store and the Union Church
keyLocations.description: The mail boat ties up at the granite wharf below the Proprietors' Store, a long grey shingled building with a porch, the post office window at one end, the store's counters, barrels and stove in the middle, and First Selectman Ellery Wyman's office and the island's records in a back room. The island's one telephone, on the submarine cable, is on the wall by the post office window, and beside it, nailed up, the year's tide table from the Coast and Geodetic Survey, with pencil marks on it. Up the slope is the white Union Church of 1873, with its square tower and an empty bell frame, and the parsonage beside it. Forty houses climb the hill behind, and nearly every one has an iron spike or a horseshoe over its door.
features: The tide table by the telephone, with five pencil crosses on it: 1 Aug, 16 Aug, 31 Aug, 15 Sept, 30 Sept, each one against the evening or night low water; nobody will say who made them (Ellery did)
The stove and its ring of chairs, where five or six old fishermen sit from four in the afternoon until supper and talk about everything except the bell, until someone buys them a plug of tobacco
The back room: the town records since 1810, the Proprietors' Record of the Gale of 1871 in Seth Wyman's hand, and the board of health minute book
The church tower: a steep ladder, a bell frame of oak beams with a cracked bearing, the bell rope coiled on a peg, and on a shelf, Zeb Lunt's ringing book; the deed box is in the parsonage
encounters: The crate: Ellery Wyman's wharf hands and Peleg Sprague, ordered by the minister to carry the bell crate up to the church, and Peg Tolman's sixty bottles clinking in the straw
The stove: the old men, who go silent when strangers come in and then, one by one, cannot help themselves
secrets: CLUE A2 (core, automatic for anyone who compares the tide table's pencil crosses with Len Garrity's claim file or with the dates people give): every crossed date is the lowest night low water of a spring tide, a day or two after a full or new moon, and every 'drowning' was within half an hour of it. Investigation DC 12: the next one on the table is Tuesday 14 October, 6:21 p.m.

CLUE A4 (core, the stove, for anyone who sits there an hour and buys the tobacco or tells a good story; Persuasion DC 13 to get it faster): 'She only rings on the big tides. Bottom of the tide. Never by day.' 'Zeb used to go up the tower and ring ours, them nights. Seemed to quiet her.' 'Nobody's been called ain't one of the old families. You notice that? Nobody's said it, but you notice.' (This last is a half-clue to Rule 2.)

CLUE A3 (core, the church tower shelf, or Kingsley Trask hands it over): Zeb Lunt's ringing book, a cloth-bound ledger, a line for every spring tide from November 1871 to May 1924: date, hour of low water, 'Rang 40 min', 'Rang 1 hr, she was slow to settle'. One line, March 1898: 'Sick. Did not ring. P. Farr lost on the flats. God forgive me.' The flyleaf has a list of names in faded ink, twenty-five of them, headed only 'Theirs' (CLUE F4 for later: it is the twenty-three of 1871, Asahel Wyman, whom the bell took in November 1871 before Joel Vining learned to answer it, and Philena Farr). Research DC 12: every date is a full or new moon.

CLUE C1 (core, the parsonage deed box, from Kingsley Trask): the Reverend Joel Vining's bequest of 1873, $400 in trust at the Rockland savings bank 'to pay a sexton to ring the bell of this church at the lowest night low water of every spring tide, by hand, and for as long as he hears the other, so long as the old bell shall ring under the sea'. Kingsley has never understood 'the other'.

CLUE D2 (Research DC 14 in the back room, or any Educated character's Seen It in a Book; Ellery refuses access unless Standing is +1 or someone has a selectman's permission, but the room's lock is old): the board of health minute book, 9 October 1871: 'Voted, that the sick of the Point and those who have tended them be removed to the Point meeting house and kept there until the fever has run, and a watch set upon the Bar.' Five signatures. The minutes for 14 to 20 October have been cut out with a knife.

CLUE E1 (automatic for anyone who asks about the iron over the doors): 'For luck.' 'My grandfather put that up.' 'Spring of '72, the year after the gale, all of them at once.' Old Mrs. Lucretia Farr, eighty-four, will not take hers down to paint the door and gets angry when asked why.

keyLocations.name: Carrow Head Light
keyLocations.description: A mile and a half east by the cart road through the spruce: a white cast-iron tower on a granite bluff, the keeper's double house, the oil house, the boat slip and the fog bell in its wooden frame with its clockwork striker. Oren Pinkham, head keeper, lives in one half of the house; the other half, the assistant's quarters, has been empty since Pottle left in September, and is Jonas Weatherby's from Friday night. The watch room at the top of the tower has the station's logbooks on a shelf, 1857 to 1924. From the gallery, by day, you can see the whole south shore, the Bar, Church Point and, at a low spring tide in clear water, a darkness on the Shelf that is the drowned church's roof.
features: The 1924 logbook, open on the watch-room desk, in Oren's square hand
The fog bell's clockwork striker, wound by a crank every four hours in thick weather, and the bell's hammer, which can be lifted off and the bell struck by hand
Pottle's note, behind the washstand in the assistant's quarters
The oilcloth bundle at the back of the logbook shelf, which Oren does not mention
encounters: Oren Pinkham, coffee pot, pipe and questions about France, which Jonas need not answer
Fog: the bell striking every twenty seconds all night, and the light turning the fog white; anyone walking the cart road at night must follow the sound
secrets: CLUE A1 (core, automatic for anyone Oren shows the 1924 log, which he will for Jonas at once and for anyone else who asks him straight; or anyone who reads it while he is asleep): 'Bell heard under water off Church Point' on 1 Aug 6:52 p.m. (L.W. 6:40), 16 Aug 6:18 p.m. (L.W. 6:05, 'ceased 6:31, another bell rung in the Harbor'), 31 Aug 6:44 p.m. (L.W. 6:33), 15 Sept 6:10 p.m. (L.W. 6:02), 30 Sept 6:58 p.m. (L.W. 6:47, 'fog bell run by request of First Selectman; no effect'). Every one within twenty minutes of the night low water of a spring tide.

CLUE C4 (core, the same log, 30 Sept, and Oren himself if asked): the fog bell's clockwork ran through the low water and Jotham Wyman was taken anyway; and on 16 Aug the drowned bell stopped when 'another bell' was rung in the Harbor at 6:29. Oren: 'Machine don't count, I'd say. Something about it wants a person.'

Pottle's note (automatic for Jonas on his first night; anyone searching the quarters): 'You hear a bell under the water on the big tides, it isn't the fog bell. Don't go down to the Point. Ask Oren about his father's log.' Oren, asked about his father's log, goes quiet and says it is 'Lighthouse Service property and no business of the island's'. He is not ready. See CLUE D1 in controlFile: he shows it in db-scenario-002, or now if the party have saved a life and asked him honestly.

From the gallery on a clear day (Perception DC 13 with the station telescope at Monday's low water, 4:52 p.m., before dark): the shadow of a roof ridge and a leaning square tower on the Shelf, under eight feet of green water, and two small buoys near it that are not lobster buoys (Galen Coombs's salt-sack markers; CLUE H3 for db-scenario-002).

keyLocations.name: Spruce Hill Burying Ground
keyLocations.description: Behind the village, a hillside of slate and marble stones among old spruces, the oldest from the 1790s. The five families have big plots with iron railings near the top: Sprague, Wyman, Coombs, Farr, Tibbetts. Lower down, the Point families' stones. Near the gate, Zebulon Lunt's fresh grave, with a wooden marker until the stone comes, and beside it his parents' slate.
features: A row of nine slate cenotaphs, stones with no graves, each reading 'LOST AT THE POINT, OCTOBER 18 1871' with a name: Thomas Grindle, Rhoda Grindle, Enos Lunt, Keziah Lunt, Oakes Ulmer, Bethia Ulmer, Dorcas Wheaton, Nathaniel Kenniston, Tryphena Kenniston; paid for, says the stonecutter's mark, by subscription of the Point families who were left
A marble stone in the Farr plot: 'Philena Farr, 1859 to 1898. Lost on the flats, March 8, 1898. The sea gave her not back.'

Three new stones and a fourth half-cut in the five families' plots: Enoch Farr, Esther Thurlow (in the Tibbetts plot, beside Aunt Hitty, paid for by the town), Jotham Wyman; and nothing at all for Clyde Tibbetts, because Verna would not order one
A bunch of wild asters on Ardelia Vining's memorial tablet, set into the church wall below, renewed every week; nobody admits to putting them there (Orpha Sprague does)
encounters: Mattie Grindle, cutting the grass on the Grindle cenotaphs with a sickle on Saturday morning, who does not want company and talks anyway
Fog, and the feeling of being watched from the spruces (an Echo of the Point dead: harmless, cold, a smell of the sea; see Dread)
secrets: CLUE B1 (core, automatic for anyone who reads the stones and the church register together; Research DC 12 to have the family trees straight in an hour, or ask Kingsley Trask): Enoch Farr, Esther Thurlow (mother a Tibbetts), Jotham Wyman, Clyde Tibbetts, Sophronia Coombs who was called and lived, and Philena Farr in 1898: every one of the five families, Sprague, Wyman, Coombs, Farr, Tibbetts, and nobody else. The same five names are on the iron-railed plots, and on the board of health minute of 1871.

Mattie Grindle's story (automatic if anyone asks her about the cenotaphs and does not argue): 'My great-grandmother and great-grandfather. They weren't sheltering. They were sick, and the Proprietors put them in the church, and they shut them in. My grandmother Lois said so every day of her life and nobody believed her because she was a Grindle and they were Spragues.' This is the first time the party hear the word 'shut'.

Zeb Lunt's grave (the Sensitive's Thin Place, or a fear check DC 10 for anyone who stands there at dusk): the impression of a tired old man climbing a ladder in the dark, two thousand times, and the feeling of relief, at last, of not having to.

keyLocations.name: The Captain's House
keyLocations.description: Highest on the hill above the Harbor, a square white house of 1840 with a widow's walk, a picket fence, a big iron horseshoe over the door, and a view of the whole bay. Orpha Sprague, seventy-three, the oldest person on Carrow, lives here with a hired woman and her great-grandson Peleg, who mostly sleeps at his boat shed. She does not go out. She does not, this week, see strangers. She watches the island from the widow's walk with her father's telescope.
features: The parlor, kept as it was in her father's time: a ship's portrait, Captain Hezekiah Sprague's chair that nobody sits in, the family Bible on a stand
The widow's walk, from which you can see the Bar, the Point and the Shelf
The hired woman, Edna Wyman's cousin Bertha, who answers the door and says 'Mrs. Sprague isn't receiving'
encounters: Orpha Sprague, if the party's Standing is +2, or if they have saved someone from the sea, or if Dr. Thurlow comes alone and says whose son he is: a ten-minute audience in the parlor, and a warning
secrets: CLUE B3 (core, from Orpha to anyone of the blood she sees; or Peleg reports it): 'You keep off the shore on the big tides, young man. You have the Tibbetts in you, like your mother, and like Esther. That's all I'll say to you, and it's all you need.' To Dr. Thurlow she adds, gently, that Esther came to see her on 14 September with a letter of her grandfather's, asking about the old church, and that Orpha 'told her nothing, God forgive me, and she went down to the water the next night'.

Orpha will not, in this scenario, say what was done. If pressed: 'I held a lantern for my father once. That's all I'll tell you.' She keeps the 1871 order in the family Bible on its stand, between Ruth and Samuel. Nobody may touch the Bible. (CLUES D5 and D6 are for db-scenario-003 and 004.)
If the party ask her how to stop the bell: 'Ring ours. By hand. Peleg knows.' She will say nothing more, but it is CLUE C2's confirmation.

keyLocations.name: Church Point and the Bar
keyLocations.description: The island's south shore, twenty minutes from the Harbor by the shore road past the Tibbetts house and Peleg Sprague's boat shed and marine railway at the head of the Bar. The Bar runs out three hundred yards across the water to Church Point, gravel and cobble and rockweed, dry for four hours either side of low water. The Point is grass and cellar holes, a fallen wall, a granite slab over the old well, and at its end a raw slope of clay and stone into deep green water. At low water on a spring tide the end of the Point is a hundred yards from the place where the church went down.
features: The head of the Bar: Peleg's boat shed, a winch, a marine railway, three dories, and a bench where the old men used to sit to watch the weirs
The cellar holes of the Point settlement, a dozen square stone pits full of raspberry canes and cold air

The capped well, uphill of which is the old curing works' offal pit, now grassed over (a Physician with Diagnosis or Medicine DC 15 who looks at both and thinks about typhoid sees why the Point was sick in 1871; for db-scenario-002)
The end of the Point: where the walkers' footprints go down into the sea
encounters: Sophronia Coombs, who walks out to the end of the Point every afternoon and stands looking at the water, and will tell what it was like to be called if someone kind asks
The ringing on Tuesday 14 October (see Act 3)
secrets: CLUE B2 (core, from Sophronia Coombs, Insight DC 10 to see she wants to talk, then kindness; or from Verna Tibbetts under pressure): 'It wasn't a bell, not to me. It was my name. Coombs, Coombs, like Mother calling me in for supper. And I was so glad. I went to answer. I wasn't sad, I wasn't anything; I was going home to tea. Then it stopped, and I was up to my knees in the sea in my nightgown, and so cold.'

CLUE G1 (Len Garrity's Careful Notes or Method, or Investigation DC 13 for anyone who asks where Clyde's boots were found and goes to look; Peleg found them): Clyde Tibbetts's sea boots were left side by side on the grass above the tide line at the end of the Point, dry inside, with his socks rolled into them; his dory was found swamped, not stove, off the Point the next morning with its oars shipped. Every other walker went into the sea fully dressed, boots and all.

The Sensitive's Thin Place at the end of the Point (DC 10 fear check for anyone else at dusk): the impression of a crowd of people, a long time ago, behind a door, and one woman's voice saying 'Come. Please come.' At the Bar's head, five small lights, like lanterns held low, that are not there when you look straight at them (five Echoes; harmless; they are always there at the bottom of a spring tide). CLUE B5: the voice is not calling the island. It is calling 'the five'.

keyLocations.name: The Tibbetts house on the shore road
keyLocations.description: Halfway between the Harbor and the Bar, a small grey Cape with a lilac by the door and an iron spike over it: Clyde and Verna Tibbetts's house, where Verna takes boarders. Further along, Aunt Hitty Tibbetts's empty house, which is now Dr. Thurlow's and his sister's estate, with Esther's suitcase still on the bed.
features: Verna's kitchen: a black range, a sugar tin on the shelf above it, a framed photograph of Clyde turned face down
Verna's front parlor, cleared for the seance: a round table, a black cloth, seven chairs, the shades drawn
Aunt Hitty's house: Esther's suitcase, her notebook, and a tin trunk of old Tibbetts papers in the attic
encounters: Verna Tibbetts, frightened, brittle and quick, who has hired Madame Perle and does not want anyone else in her house on Sunday night
The seance on Sunday night (see Act 2)
secrets: CLUE G2 (Investigation DC 14 in Verna's kitchen, or Sleight of Hand, or simply being alone in it; Pearl Haverty is boarding there): in the sugar tin, $300 in new Canadian banknotes and a letter postmarked Saint-Pierre et Miquelon, 22 Sept, unsigned: 'All well aboard. Stay put till the money comes. Burn this.' She has not burned it.

CLUE C3 (Verna, when confronted with G1 or G2, or with Cold Reading and kindness): 'He was called. On the thirty-first. I heard him say our name, Tibbetts, Tibbetts, and he went for the door. I held him. I held him on the shore with my arms round him and my heels in the gravel, and it took all I had, and when the tide turned he stopped and looked at me and said, Verna, what are we doing out here? So you can hold them. You can.' She will then beg the party not to tell Galen Coombs or the insurance man that Clyde is alive.

Esther's notebook in Aunt Hitty's house (automatic for Dr. Thurlow; Research DC 12 for anyone else): notes on a letter she found in the attic trunk from Eliphalet Tibbetts, her great-grandfather, to his brother in Belfast, Maine, dated November 1871: 'We did what we thought right for the island's sake and God has shown us otherwise. I cannot write it. Ask me nothing when I come.' Under it, in Esther's hand: 'Ask Mrs. Sprague. Old church. Fever?' The Eliphalet letter is in the trunk (a half-clue to D, for later).

synopsis: The party come out to Carrow on the Friday mail boat, in fog, with the recast church bell in a crate in the hold and Peg Tolman's whisky in the straw around it. The island receives them politely and tells them nothing. Over five days they can learn, from the lighthouse log, the tide table by the store telephone and the sexton's ringing book, that the drowned bell rings only at the lowest night low water of each spring tide, and that the next is Tuesday 14 October at 6:21 p.m. From the burying ground, the church register, an old fisherman's half-sentence and Orpha Sprague's warning, they can learn that it calls only the blood of the five old Proprietor families. And from a dead minister's bequest, the night Peleg Sprague rang the church bell in secret, the night the lighthouse fog bell's clockwork failed to answer, a ballad's second verse and Verna Tibbetts's confession that she held her husband on the shore until the tide turned, they can learn that it can be answered by a bell rung by hand, and that the called can be held. Meanwhile Len Garrity's insurance case turns up one real fraud: Clyde Tibbetts is alive on a Saint-Pierre rum schooner, and his wife has hired Pearl Haverty to hold a seance to prove him dead, at which something real speaks instead. On Tuesday the party must hang the new bell in the church tower and ring it by hand for as long as the drowned bell rings, and hold whoever is called, Peleg Sprague, Sophronia Coombs or Dr. Thurlow himself, back from the sea until the tide turns. If they do, nobody walks into the sea for the first time since July, the island's Standing for them rises, Orpha Sprague sends for them, and they learn that in two weeks there will be a tide so low that the drowned church will stand out of the water, and that on that tide, she says, it will call every one of the blood at once.
hook: Friday morning, the Rockland wharf, then three hours of fog. When the bell rings under the boat halfway out, Captain Stinson says it is not the right tide for her and keeps going. When the mail boat ties up at Carrow, the islanders on the wharf look at the six strangers and at the crate, and the young minister, Kingsley Trask, comes running down the hill in his overshoes, delighted, to welcome his bell. Peg Tolman has perhaps ten minutes before eight men pick the crate up and something inside it clinks.

conclusions.conclusion: A. The bell rings at the lowest night low water of each spring tide (Rule 1), and the next is Tuesday 14 October at 6:21 p.m.
clues: A1: the 1924 lighthouse log, each ringing within twenty minutes of the night low water (Carrow Head Light)
A2: the tide table's pencil crosses against the claim file's dates (the Store)
A3: Zeb Lunt's ringing book, fifty-two years of full and new moons (the church tower)
A4: the old men at the stove: 'bottom of the tide, never by day' (the Store)

conclusions.conclusion: B. It calls only the blood of the five Proprietor families (Rule 2)
clues: B1: the stones and the register: every walker since 1898 a Sprague, Wyman, Coombs, Farr or Tibbetts (Spruce Hill, the church)
B2: Sophronia Coombs heard her own family name (Church Point)
B3: Orpha Sprague's warning to the doctor: 'You have the Tibbetts in you' (the Captain's House)
B5: the Sensitive at the Point: it is calling 'the five' (Church Point)
B6: the ballad's third verse, if Imogen Lisle finds it (see Act 2)

conclusions.conclusion: C. It can be answered by a bell rung by hand, and the called can be held until the tide turns (Rule 3)
clues: C1: Joel Vining's bequest, 'by hand, and for as long as he hears the other' (the parsonage deed box)
C2: Peleg Sprague rang on 16 August and nobody was taken (Peleg, Orpha, the 1924 log)
C3: Verna Tibbetts held Clyde on the shore until the tide turned (the Tibbetts house)
C4: the fog bell's clockwork did not answer on 30 September (the Light)
C5: the ballad's second verse, 'ring her an answer, ring her by hand' (Imogen Lisle's cylinder)

conclusions.conclusion: G. Clyde Tibbetts is alive (the one real fraud)
clues: G1: the dry boots and the swamped dory (Church Point)
G2: the Canadian banknotes and the Saint-Pierre letter in the sugar tin (the Tibbetts house)
G3: Peg Tolman saw him on the Bonne Chance's deck in September (Peg)
G4: Verna's seance script, and what came instead (the seance)

acts.title: Friday: The Mail Boat
acts.description: The crossing, the arrival, the crate and the first night. The point of this act is to put the party on the island with the clock showing, to introduce the island as decent people with a weight on them, and to let each pregen's reason for coming collide with the others' on the wharf. Lodgings: Pearl Haverty and Imogen Lisle at Verna Tibbetts's; Len Garrity in the room over the Store, let by Ellery's wife Edna; Dr. Thurlow at Aunt Hitty's empty house; Jonas Weatherby at the Light; Peg Tolman wherever Galen Coombs has arranged, which is the loft of Peleg's boat shed. Any of them can change.
objectives: Get ashore, and get the crate up to the church without the minister finding the whisky, or decide to let him
Meet the island: the Store, the minister, the First Selectman, the old men at the stove
Learn that three people have been 'drowned' since August, and that the island will not discuss it
Jonas Weatherby reports to Carrow Head Light and finds Pottle's note

scenes.name: Fog on the Bay
scenes.description: The three-hour crossing on the Viola R. A chance for the pregens to meet in the cramped cabin over Captain Stinson's coffee, and to find out who is going to Carrow and why: Len Garrity recognises Dr. Thurlow's name from his claim file and Pearl Haverty's face from a photograph of Professor Orr's seance room; Pearl recognises Len from the same newspaper; Peg Tolman keeps an eye on her crate; Imogen Lisle asks everyone if they know any songs. Halfway out, the drowned bell: a single deep stroke, then three more, felt through the planking more than heard. It is not a spring low, and it does not call anyone; it is a sign (it rings faintly, once, whenever anyone of the blood crosses the water toward Carrow, which only Dr. Thurlow is). Stinson keeps going and says it is not the right tide for her.
scenes.readAloud: The fog comes down on you a mile out of Rockland and never lifts. The Viola R. puts along through it at half speed, her one-lung engine thudding like a slow heart, and the world is twenty yards of flat grey water in every direction and then nothing. Captain Stinson stands at the wheel with his pipe out and steers by the compass and by a sound you begin to hear after the second hour: a bell, off to the east, slow and patient, one stroke every twenty seconds. 'Carrow Head,' he says. 'Fog bell.' Then, under it, something else. Not from the east. From below. A single deep note that you feel in the soles of your feet before you hear it, as if the boat had passed over a church tower, and then three more, slower, fainter, falling away behind you. Nobody speaks. Stinson does not slow down. 'Tide's not right for her,' he says, to nobody in particular. 'She only rings on the big tides. You'll be hearing things. Everybody does, first time.'

skillChecks.success: A bell. Sound carries strangely over water in fog; you have heard church bells across a lake at night that seemed to come from under it. You file it away.
skillChecks.failure: It is the sound of a bell under your feet, under the sea, and for a moment you are sure the boat is going to stop, and you will have to look over the side. Gain 1 Dread. (Pearl Haverty hears, under it, a woman's voice say 'Come. Please come.' She gains the Dread whether she saves or not, and nobody else hears it.)

skillChecks.success: Stinson is not surprised and not as calm as he pretends. He has heard it before on this run, and he will not bring the boat to Carrow on the evening of a big tide for any money. If asked, he says the island's been 'ringing' since August and it's none of his business, and then, quietly: 'Don't go down to the Point on Tuesday.'
skillChecks.failure: Stinson is an old Maine skipper who has heard everything and believes half of it. He tells you a story about a sea serpent off Monhegan and laughs at it.

skillChecks.success: Dr. Thurlow is the only one of you who flinched before the first stroke, not after it, as if he heard it a moment sooner than anyone else. (He did. He is of the blood.)
skillChecks.failure: Everyone looks as pale as everyone else.

scenes.name: The Bell for the Church
scenes.description: The wharf. Kingsley Trask, overjoyed, has organised eight men to carry his bell up to the church on poles; Ellery Wyman, stiff and civil, wants to know who the strangers are and what they want, and makes clear that Carrow 'has had about enough of people from away coming to look at our trouble'. Peg Tolman has a problem: sixty quart bottles of rye are packed in the straw around the bell, the crate is consigned to the church, and the minister has a crowbar. Let Peg's player solve it with the others or alone: a distraction while she and Peleg (who knows exactly what is in the crate, because Galen Coombs told him to meet the boat) unpack 'the straw' into a fish barrel; a quiet word with Galen's man on the wharf; or a confession to the minister, who will be shocked, and then, surprisingly, practical about it ('I would rather you did not do this in my church, Miss Tolman, but I would very much rather have my bell'). If the whisky is found in public, Standing -1 and Ellery threatens to telephone the Coast Guard; Galen Coombs smooths it over by evening, because it is his whisky now. The island watches all of it.
scenes.readAloud: The fog opens on a granite wharf, a long grey store with a porch, a row of white houses climbing a hill into the murk, and a church with a square tower and an empty belfry. There are twenty people on the wharf, waiting for the mail, and every one of them is looking at you. Then a tall young man in a clerical collar and rubber overshoes comes running down the hill waving his hat, shouting 'Is it here? Is it here?', and the islanders step aside for him with the faces of people who are fond of a puppy. 'My bell,' he says to Captain Stinson, 'my bell, my bell,' and then he sees the crate being swung up out of the hold, eight feet long and stencilled HANDLE WITH CARE, and his face lights up like Christmas morning. Behind him a heavy, grey, clean-shaven man in a store apron says, 'Afternoon. Ellery Wyman. I'm First Selectman. You'll be wanting rooms, I expect. You'll be wanting to know what you've come for, too, and I'd as soon you asked me as went round asking everybody else.' The crate comes down onto the wharf with a thump, and from somewhere inside the straw, very faintly, something clinks.

skillChecks.success: In the confusion of eight men, two poles and a minister, the straw and what is in it goes into a fish barrel that Peleg Sprague just happens to have on a handcart. Nobody notices but Ellery Wyman, who notices everything and decides to say nothing until he knows what you are.
skillChecks.failure: A bottle slides out of the straw, rolls across the wharf planks and stops at Ellery Wyman's boot. There is a long silence. Then one of the old men at the back starts to laugh, and keeps laughing. Standing -1 with Ellery; +1 with the young men of the Harbor.

skillChecks.success: Ellery Wyman will give you rooms, sell you anything in the Store, and answer one question straight: 'Three drowned since August. Enoch Farr, Jotham Wyman, who was my brother, and Hitty Tibbetts's niece from Boston. Clyde Tibbetts too, they say. It's the tide and the dark and the cold, and there's been talk of a bell, and I'll thank you not to add to it.' He is grieving, and he means it.
skillChecks.failure: Ellery gives you rooms and nothing else. 'We don't talk about our trouble to the papers, or the insurance, or the Coast Guard, or anybody from away. That's all.'

skillChecks.success: Ellery is not hiding a crime; he is hiding a fear he does not understand. When he said 'my brother' his hand went to the iron spike over the Store door, as if he meant to touch it for luck, and stopped.
skillChecks.failure: A stiff, cold Yankee storekeeper who does not like you. The island is full of them.

scenes.name: The Keeper's Kitchen
scenes.description: Jonas Weatherby reports to Carrow Head Light at dusk, and anyone who walks out with him is welcome to supper: Oren Pinkham fries haddock, pours coffee, and talks about everything, the light, the fog bell, the ledges, his late wife Abbie, the Lighthouse Service, France if Jonas will let him, which he probably will not. He shows Jonas the station and the logbooks as a matter of duty. If anyone asks about the bell, he looks at them for a while and then turns the 1924 log round on the table so they can read it (CLUE A1, CLUE C4). That night, in the assistant's quarters, Jonas finds Pottle's note. In the small hours the fog bell's clockwork runs down and must be rewound; Oren lets Jonas do it alone, to see how he does.
scenes.readAloud: The keeper's kitchen at Carrow Head is the warmest room on the island: a black range with the oven door open, a kettle, a coffee pot that is never quite empty, oilcloth on the table, geraniums on the sill, a barometer on the wall, and a short round red-faced man in a darned reefer who shakes your hand as if he has been waiting for you all week. 'Oren Pinkham. You'll be Weatherby. Aroostook, they said. You won't talk much, then. Good. Sit. There's haddock.' Above the table the light turns in its iron tower, and every ten seconds a pale sweep goes over the window and turns the fog outside to white smoke. Out on the bluff the fog bell strikes, and strikes, and strikes. Somewhere under the sound of it, if you listen, is the sea, breathing in and out on the rocks below.

skillChecks.success: Oren likes you. He shows you the 1924 log without being asked, and then says, very quietly, 'My father kept a log too. I'll show you that one some day, maybe. Not tonight.' He will be your friend on the island from now on.
skillChecks.failure: Oren is friendly and tells you a great deal about kerosene vapor lamps. When you ask about the bell, he says 'It's in the log' and changes the subject.

skillChecks.success: The fog bell's clockwork is an old weight-driven striker with a governor; you can rewind it, adjust it, and, if you think of it, lift off the hammer so the bell can be struck by hand with a mallet. Oren grunts approval.
skillChecks.failure: The crank slips and the weight drops a foot with a bang that wakes Oren. He comes out in his nightshirt and shows you, patiently.

skillChecks.success: Pottle's note is a frightened man's note. You fold it and put it in your pocket and go to bed, and sleep, mostly.
skillChecks.failure: You read Pottle's note twice, and then you lie awake listening to the fog bell and waiting for the other one. Gain 1 Dread.

encounters: The wharf and the crate: a social scene with eight islanders, a minister, a First Selectman and sixty bottles of rye; no fighting unless someone makes it
Galen Coombs's man on the wharf, Arno Farr (use Night Watchman statistics), who has come to make sure Peg's 'barrel of salt fish' reaches Sculpin Cove, and who is polite until someone touches it

acts.title: Saturday to Monday: The Island Talks, and Doesn't
acts.description: Three days of investigation, the island's ordinary life, and a seance. The fog lifts on Sunday in a hard northwest wind. The party can go anywhere on the island in an hour; the clues for Rules 1 to 3 are in the Store, the Light, the church tower and parsonage, Spruce Hill, the Captain's House, Church Point and the Tibbetts house. Let each player follow their pregen's reason for coming: Imogen her ballad, Len his claims, Nathan his sister, Peg her buyer, Jonas his light, Pearl her seance. The island's set pieces happen on their own: the Grange supper and dance on Saturday night, where everyone is and the young men drink Galen's whisky behind the hall; Jotham Wyman's memorial service on Sunday morning with an empty coffin, where Kingsley Trask preaches badly and honestly about the sea; Verna Tibbetts's seance on Sunday night; the Monday mail boat, which anyone can take to Rockland and which will not bring them back until Wednesday, after the ringing, and the GM should say so. Standing moves all weekend.
objectives: Learn when the bell rings (Rule 1) and that it rings again on Tuesday at 6:21 p.m.
Learn whom it calls (Rule 2), and realise that Peleg, Sophronia and Dr. Thurlow are all of the blood
Learn how it can be answered and how the called can be held (Rule 3)
Hold, expose or quietly survive the seance; discover that Clyde Tibbetts is alive
Find the rest of Imogen Lisle's ballad

scenes.name: The Rest of the Song
scenes.description: Imogen Lisle's thread. Zeb Lunt is dead, but his late brother's widow, Thankful Lunt, eighty, is alive and lives with her daughter in the Harbor, and she sang with Zeb in the church choir for fifty years. She knows four verses of 'The Carrow Bell', and will sing three of them into the phonograph horn if Imogen is kind, patient and sings one first. The fourth she will not sing at all, not on the island, 'not while there's a Sprague alive to hear it', and she says that Zeb wrote it down in the back of his ringing book, which he did, on the inside back cover, upside down (CLUE F1; Imogen can find it now, if she looks, or in db-scenario-002). The third verse is CLUE B6. With Thankful's verses and the two Imogen has, the ballad is all there except the end.
scenes.readAloud: Thankful Lunt is very small and very upright in a rocking chair by a kitchen window full of geraniums, with a shawl round her and her hands folded on a cane, and she looks at the phonograph horn as if it might bite. 'Zeb wrote to you,' she says. 'He said a young lady was coming from Harvard College for the old song. I told him he was a fool.' She is quiet for a long time. Then she shuts her eyes, and in a thin, true, cracked old voice that has sung in the Union Church choir since Lincoln was president, she begins, and you set the cylinder turning. 'Oh, the sea came over Carrow Bar, the night the Point went down, and the bell rang out from the meeting house to the lanterns on the town. Ring her an answer, ring her by hand, when the moon is full or new; ring her an answer from the land, and she'll sleep the whole tide through.' She stops, and opens her eyes, and looks at you. 'There's more,' she says. 'You won't like it.' And then, very low: 'Oh, she calls them home by their fathers' names, the Farr and the Wyman sons, the Sprague and the Tibbetts and Coombs's blood, for the five that held the guns.' She will not sing the last.

skillChecks.success: You sing her a verse of something old first, a ballad she half knows from her mother, and she smiles for the first time and sings you three. The cylinder holds them all. (CLUES B6 and C5.)
skillChecks.failure: She sings the first two verses, the ones everyone knows, and then says she is tired. Come back tomorrow, with something better than a machine.

skillChecks.success: She tells you why she won't sing the last verse on the island: 'Because it says what they did, and there's Spragues in the next house.' And then: 'Zeb wrote it in the back of his book. Upside down, so the minister wouldn't see.' (Points to CLUE F1.)
skillChecks.failure: 'Some songs ain't for collecting, dear.' She will not be moved today.

skillChecks.success: 'For the five that held the guns' is wrong, and she knows it; she changed the word as she sang it. The verse she learned said something else. (Imogen's Ear for the song: the original line is 'for the five that held the doors'. Imogen's Folklorist tradition gives this without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: A beautiful, frightening old song. You will be writing about it for years.

scenes.name: Three Claims and No Bodies
scenes.description: Len Garrity's thread, and Dr. Thurlow's, which run into each other. Len wants statements: from the two fishermen who saw Esther walk into the sea (Elisha Coombs and young Frank Wyman, who tried to reach her in a dory and could not: 'She didn't splash. She just walked, and the water came up, and then it was over her hat'); from Ellery about Jotham; from Verna about Clyde, which goes badly; and from Dr. Thurlow, whom he suspects as a matter of routine and who finds out. Nathan wants his sister. Let them clash, and then let them notice that Esther's death looks exactly like Enoch's and Jotham's and nothing like Clyde's. The seventh pencil mark is Clyde's 'drowning' on 2 September: it is not on a spring tide, and nobody heard the bell. That is the first crack in the case for Len, and the first time There's an Explanation turns out to be right.
scenes.readAloud: Elisha Coombs is sixty and has fished out of Carrow Harbor for fifty years, and he sits on an upturned trap at the head of the wharf, mending a net with a wooden needle, and does not look up while he talks. 'Fifteenth September. Evening, dark, flat calm. Me and Frankie Wyman was coming in late from the weir. Saw her on the Point, in the lantern, Hitty Tibbetts's niece, the schoolteacher, in her stocking feet. Walking. Not running. We hollered and she didn't turn round. We got the dory over and pulled for her and she was in to her knees and then her waist and then she was swimming, or something like it, out toward the Shelf, steady, like she knew where she was going. And then her hat. And then nothing.' He stops. He pulls the needle through. 'And under all of it, the bell. Under the water. I heard it plain as I hear you. I'd like to know what kind of a policy you write for that, mister.'

skillChecks.success: You lay the four cases side by side. Enoch, Esther, Jotham: a spring low water, the bell heard, walked into the sea fully dressed, seen by witnesses, never found. Clyde: a neap tide two days after a ringing, nobody heard anything, nobody saw him go, boots left dry on the grass. One of these is not like the others. (Leads to CLUES G1 and G2.)
skillChecks.failure: Four drownings on one island in eight weeks. Rum-runners, liquor, the cold, a family with a weak heart. The explanations pile up and none of them fits all four.

skillChecks.success: Dr. Thurlow is not a man after $3,000; he is a man after his sister. And Elisha Coombs is telling the plain truth, and is more frightened of what he saw than of anything that could be done to him for saying it.
skillChecks.failure: Everybody on this island has a reason to lie to an insurance man. That's all you're sure of.

skillChecks.success: Dr. Thurlow examines Sophronia Coombs, who was called and lived: she is perfectly healthy, has no history of sleepwalking, fits or drink, and her pulse goes up when she talks about it the way a pulse goes up at the memory of joy. Whatever this is, it is not an illness. (Diagnosis gives this without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: A healthy woman of forty who was found in the sea at dawn. You can find nothing wrong with her, and that is worse.

scenes.name: Madame Perle
scenes.description: Sunday night, Verna Tibbetts's darkened parlor, seven chairs: Verna, Pearl, two or three neighbor women Verna has invited to witness, and any of the party who can get a seat (Pearl can invite them; Verna does not want Len Garrity there and will say so). Verna's script asks 'Clyde' to say he drowned peacefully, the bell called him, he forgives everyone, and Verna should take the insurance and go to her sister's in Belfast. The neighbors are there so that Galen Coombs hears it by morning. Pearl can perform the con, refuse it, or change it. Whatever she does, about ten minutes in, the real thing arrives: not Clyde, who is alive, but Ardelia Vining, the bell's ringer. The lamp gutters and will not stay lit. The room smells of the sea. Water seeps under the parlor door from nowhere. The little bell on its thread, which Pearl has not touched, begins to ring by itself, slowly, and will not stop. Pearl, if she lets herself (The Thin Place, Listener), hears a woman's voice, very close, say: 'Not him. He is not with us. He is alive, and he is a coward. We are twenty-three. Come. Please come. The door.' Then it is gone, and the neighbors are screaming, and Verna is white, because she knows exactly what it meant. Run it as quiet and slow as possible until it is not.
scenes.readAloud: The lamp is turned down to a bead of blue, and the parlor is close and warm and smells of lamp oil and the neighbors' camphor. Seven hands on a black cloth. Madame Perle's voice, low and French and confident, asking the spirits to come forward, asking for Clyde, Clyde Tibbetts, who was lost to the sea. A rap, under the table, very convincing. Verna Tibbetts's breath catching. Then the lamp goes out. Not down: out, though nobody touched it. And in the dark the room is suddenly cold, wet cold, the cold of a cellar with the sea in it, and there is a smell of rockweed, and something is moving across the floor under the table, round your feet, around your ankles: water, ice-cold, rising. Somewhere very close a small bell begins to ring, slowly, one stroke, and then another, and another, like a bell rope being pulled by someone who is very tired and will not stop.

skillChecks.success: It is happening, and you do not know what it is, and you keep your hands on the cloth and your eyes open. You see Pearl Haverty's face in the dark by the light of nothing at all, and she is not acting.
skillChecks.failure: You are out of your chair and against the wall before you know you have moved, and the water is round your shoes. Gain 1 Dread. (Pearl, if she opens herself, gains her point of Dread from The Thin Place, and hears the voice.)

skillChecks.success: Verna Tibbetts is more frightened than anyone in the room, and not of the ghost: of what it said. 'He is alive.' She knows. (Leads to CLUES G2, C3.)
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is frightened. Two of the neighbor women are praying.

skillChecks.success: Afterwards, with the lamp lit: Pearl's clicker and trumpet are in her bag, untouched. The water on the floor is salt, and there is weed in it. The little bell's thread runs to nothing. Len Garrity, if he is here, has to decide what he saw. (Debunker does not make him succeed on this fear check: this was not a trick.)
skillChecks.failure: Salt water on a parlor floor. Somebody could have brought it in a bucket. Somebody could have.

encounters: The Grange supper and dance, Saturday night: the whole island, a fiddle and a piano, beans and brown bread, Galen Coombs's whisky behind the hall, and a chance for Standing +1 if the party dance, eat and do not ask about the bell

Galen Coombs and two of his men (Night Watchman statistics), who come to Peg Tolman on Saturday night for the whisky, pay $1,800 in cash, and want to know who the other strangers are, especially the insurance man and the lighthouse keeper; a fight here is a mistake
The seance (no combat; the presence cannot be fought and leaves on its own; Ardelia Vining's full statistics are in db-scenario-002)
A Coast Guard 75-foot patrol boat noses into the Harbor on Monday morning, asks the Store about 'a woman named Tolman', and leaves; Peg's Standing with Galen depends on what the island tells them

acts.title: Tuesday 14 October: The Bottom of the Tide
acts.description: The ringing. Tuesday is bright and cold, the wind gone into the southwest, and the island quiet all day. Sunset is at 4:58; it is full dark by 5:40; the low water is at 6:21 p.m.; the drowned bell will ring from about 6:05 until about 6:40, and the tide turns at about 6:45. The party have two jobs, and should split up to do them. First, the answer: the recast bell must be hung in the church tower and rung by hand for as long as the drowned bell rings. Hanging it needs Peleg's block and tackle, three hours and a strong crew: start by early afternoon. Ringing it means forty minutes on the rope (Rites That Work: a Constitution save DC 10 every five minutes, rising by 2, with a second ringer to take over). If the recast bell is not hung, a ship's bell from the wharf, the school handbell or the fog bell at the Head struck by hand will do. Second, the called: the drowned bell calls the one of the blood nearest Church Point when it begins. If Dr. Thurlow has gone down to the Point to see where his sister walked, which he very likely has, it is him; otherwise Peleg Sprague, in his boat shed at the head of the Bar, unless he is in the church tower ringing, in which case Sophronia Coombs, in the last house on the shore road. The called hears their family name and walks, steadily, toward the end of the Point and the water. The answer stops the call only when it starts and only while it lasts; the minutes before the answering bell starts, and any lapse in it, the called walks. Someone has to hold them.
objectives: Hang the recast bell in the church tower, or find another bell, and ring it by hand for as long as the drowned bell rings
Hold whoever is called back from the sea until the tide turns
Do not let anyone go into the water after the called
Afterwards, be sent for by Orpha Sprague

scenes.name: Raising the Bell
scenes.description: Afternoon in the church tower: Peleg Sprague, Kingsley Trask, and whoever will help. The bell is nine hundred pounds of new bronze; the oak frame's bearing is cracked; the tower ladder is steep and the trap is narrow. Peleg rigs a block and tackle from the tower's top beam and they haul it up through the trap foot by foot. Let it be a heavy, sweaty, funny, nervous scene, with the light going outside the louvers and the islanders gathering in the churchyard below to watch, some of them helping without being asked. If it goes badly, the bell is hung crooked and rings with a crack in its voice, which works just as well. If it goes very badly (two failed checks), it is still on the tower floor at five, and the party must find another bell.
scenes.readAloud: The bell comes out of its straw into the grey light of the churchyard, and for a moment everyone stops: a great green-gold cup of new bronze as tall as a man's chest, with letters cast round its waist, RICKER FOUNDRY EAST BOSTON 1924, and below them, in older letters copied from the cracked bell it was cast from, the words the island chose in 1873: I RING FOR THE LIVING AND FOR THE LOST. Kingsley Trask touches it with one finger and it hums. Then Peleg Sprague says 'Well, she won't climb that ladder by herself,' and throws a rope over the beam, and the long cold afternoon begins.

skillChecks.success: Hand over hand, with Peg Tolman's Heavy Work and three islanders on the fall, the bell goes up through the trap and swings into the frame. Peleg pins the bearings. It is hung by four o'clock. Standing +1: half the Harbor saw you do it.
skillChecks.failure: The fall slips, the bell drops a yard and stops with a jerk that cracks the trap's frame; nobody is hurt, everybody is frightened, and it is half past four before it is in.

skillChecks.success: You see that the cracked bearing will not take a ringing bell's swing; you shim it with a hardwood wedge and an iron strap from the boat shed. It will hold for one night. (Peleg or Peg's Grease Under the Nails sees it without a roll.)
skillChecks.failure: The bell is hung, but the bearing groans at every swing. It will hold, mostly. Give the ringer disadvantage on the first Constitution save.

skillChecks.success: The bell's inscription, I RING FOR THE LIVING AND FOR THE LOST, is only words. You keep hauling.
skillChecks.failure: As the bell clears the trap it swings, and touches the frame, and gives a single soft note, and from far off to the south, under the sea, very faintly, another bell answers it, an hour and a half too early. Gain 1 Dread. Everyone in the tower heard it.

scenes.name: The Ringing
scenes.description: 6:05 p.m. The drowned bell begins: heard all over the island, under the sea, deep and slow. At the head of the Bar or on the Point, the called stands up, says their family name aloud in a pleased, surprised voice, and walks toward the water at a steady pace. They do not run, do not speak, do not look sad; they are answering. Anyone who tries to stop them is in a contest (Rites That Work: a contested Athletics check each round, the called at +4, never trying to hurt anyone). The water at the end of the Point is two hundred yards from the head of the Bar; at walking pace that is three minutes. In the tower, the answering ringer starts when they hear the drowned bell, and from the moment the answer begins, the called stops walking and stands, swaying, listening to two bells, for as long as the answer goes on; if it falters, they walk again. Five small lights stand at the head of the Bar, lantern height, and do not move (five Echoes). If the called reaches the water and goes in, they can still be pulled out in the first two rounds (Athletics DC 12, and a fear check DC 15 for whoever goes in after them; the sea is very cold, and something under the water is pulling the other way). After that they are gone. When the tide turns at 6:45 the drowned bell stops, and the called sits down on the gravel and asks what everyone is doing out here.
scenes.readAloud: At five minutes past six, in the full dark, with the tide at the bottom and the Bar lying out across the water like a road, it begins. Not loud. Deep. A single stroke from somewhere off the end of the Point, under the sea, that comes up through the gravel into your boots and through your ribs into your chest, and then another, slow, and another, steady as a heartbeat, as a bell rope pulled by somebody who has been pulling it for a very long time. Up in the Harbor every lamp is lit and every door is shut. Out at the head of the Bar, five small yellow lights you did not see a moment ago stand in a row, lantern height, perfectly still, looking out toward the Point. And beside you, someone you know stands up, with a look on their face you have never seen on it, surprised and glad, like someone who has heard a voice they love calling them in from a field, and says their own family name, aloud, softly, as if answering it. And begins to walk.

skillChecks.success: You see it and you do not freeze. You go after them. (Knowing any of the bell's rules lowers this DC by 2, per dread.json: DC 13 for a party that has done its homework.)
skillChecks.failure: For a moment you cannot move, and the called is ten yards further down the Bar before you can. Gain 1 Dread.

skillChecks.success: You get your arms round them and your heels in the gravel and hold, and they lean against you toward the sea like a man against a gale, and do not fight you, and do not stop. Hold for the rounds until the answering bell starts or the tide turns. (This is the contested check: the called rolls Athletics at +4. Mattie Grindle's Longshoreman and Peg's Heavy Work give advantage; two holders each roll and the called must beat both.)
skillChecks.failure: They walk through your arms as if you were a curtain, gently, and keep going. You can try again next round, if you can catch them.

skillChecks.success: In the tower, the rope burns your hands and your shoulders are on fire and you keep ringing, and keep ringing, and somewhere far off the other bell is listening. Each five minutes, the DC rises by 2; a second ringer can take over.
skillChecks.failure: Your arms give out and the bell's swing dies and for a few terrible seconds there is only one bell on Carrow, under the sea, and out on the Bar the called starts walking again. Someone has to take the rope.

scenes.name: The Turn of the Tide
scenes.description: 6:45 p.m. The drowned bell stops in the middle of a stroke. The called comes back to themselves, cold and shaking and full of a joy they cannot explain and that drains out of them as they understand what happened. The five lights at the head of the Bar are gone. Up in the Harbor, door after door opens, and the islanders come down the hill with lanterns in a long line, because they heard two bells tonight, and nobody walked, and nothing like that has happened since Zeb Lunt died. If someone was saved, the island's Standing for the party rises by 2, Ellery Wyman shakes hands with them in front of everyone, and on Wednesday morning Bertha comes down from the Captain's House to say that Mrs. Sprague will see them at eleven. If someone was taken, the island's silence closes over it like water, Ellery Wyman does not look at them, and Orpha Sprague sends for Dr. Thurlow alone. Either way Orpha's audience gives the party CLUE B3 if they do not have it, confirms Rule 3 ('Ring ours. By hand. Every big tide. That's what Zeb did, and that's what you must do'), and delivers the scenario's last news: 'In two weeks the moon is new and near, and Oren Pinkham will tell you the glass is going to fall. It'll be a tide such as nobody living has seen. The sea will give back the Point. And when it does, she'll call all of us at once. Every one of the blood. Mr. Vining told me so, the year he left, and I never knew him wrong.' She will not say how he knew.
scenes.readAloud: The other bell stops. Not fading: stopping, in the middle of a stroke, the way a bell stops when a hand is put flat against it. The silence afterwards is enormous. The sea breathes on the Bar. Somewhere up in the Harbor a dog barks. And the one you were holding goes slack in your arms, and sits down suddenly on the wet gravel, and looks up at you in the light of your lantern, shivering so hard their teeth knock, and says, in an ordinary, puzzled, frightened voice, 'What are we doing out here?' Then the lanterns start coming down the hill from the Harbor, one and then three and then twenty, a long swinging line of them on the shore road, and the islanders, who have heard two bells tonight and seen nobody walk into the sea, come down to the Bar in their nightclothes and their oilskins and their Sunday coats, without a word, to see who you are.

skillChecks.success: Wrap them in blankets, get them to a stove, hot coffee with sugar, and keep talking to them. They will be well by morning, and they will remember everything. (Dr. Thurlow's Steady Hands and Treat Shock work here; if he was the one called, someone else must do this for him.)
skillChecks.failure: They are very cold and shaking badly; it takes two hours at the Store stove to bring them round, and they gain 1 Dread.

skillChecks.success: In front of the lanterns you say the right thing, plainly: that it can be answered, that it will be answered every big tide from now on, that nobody else needs to walk. The island hears you. Standing +1 more, and Ellery Wyman says, in front of everyone, 'They can have the back room. They can have anything they want.'
skillChecks.failure: You say too much, or the wrong thing ('ghost', 'curse', 'insurance'), and the lanterns go back up the hill without a word. The island is grateful and afraid of you.

skillChecks.success: Ellery Wyman, in the lantern light, looks out at the Point with the face of a man who has just understood that his brother did not need to die, and that the reason has something to do with his own family. He will not say it. He knows it now.
skillChecks.failure: Relief, cold and fear on every face. That is all the lantern light shows.

encounters: The called (Peleg Sprague, Dr. Thurlow or Sophronia Coombs): not an enemy; a contested Athletics check each round to hold them, the called at +4; they never harm anyone
Five Echoes at the head of the Bar (CR 0 spirits, harmless; a fear check DC 10 to see them); attacking them does nothing

If someone goes into the water after the called: the sea at 50 degrees, a current setting toward the Shelf, and something pulling; Athletics DC 12 to get back out each round, and a level of exhaustion for every two rounds in the water

npcsInvolved.name: Captain Solon Stinson, 66
npcsInvolved.role: Skipper of the mail boat Viola R.
npcsInvolved.description: Lean, brown, bald under a cloth cap, a pipe he never lights at sea, a Knox County mail contract and thirty years on the Carrow run. Takes anything and anybody and asks nothing. Will not bring the boat to Carrow on the evening of a spring low water.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Keep the contract, keep the boat, keep out of island business.

npcsInvolved.name: Ellery Wyman, 58
npcsInvolved.role: First Selectman, keeper of the Proprietors' Store and the island's records
npcsInvolved.description: Heavy, grey, clean-shaven, store apron, gold watch chain, a slow careful voice. Married to Edna; one grown son in the Navy. His younger brother Jotham walked into the sea on 30 September while the fog bell's clockwork ran. He told the minister in July to 'do as you think best' about the ringing, and knows now what that cost.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Hold the island together, keep strangers and newspapers out of it, and not find out what his grandfather did. Grief makes him hard.

npcsInvolved.name: Orpha Sprague, 73
npcsInvolved.role: The oldest person on Carrow; the last witness of 1871
npcsInvolved.description: Tiny, very straight, white hair in a knot, black silk, her father's telescope and her father's eyes. Sharp, dry, formidable and, under it, worn through. Watches the island from the widow's walk. Puts asters on Ardelia Vining's tablet every week.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep her great-grandson alive, and the island's families from being destroyed by the truth, which she is beginning to understand are not the same wish.

npcsInvolved.name: Verna Tibbetts, 31
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, dark, quick, pretty and tired, a Rockland woman who married onto the island at twenty. Takes boarders. Has $300 in a sugar tin and a husband on a rum schooner.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Get the insurance, get off the island, get to Saint-Pierre and Clyde, and never be called upon to hold anyone on a shore in the dark again.

npcsInvolved.name: Sophronia Coombs, 40
npcsInvolved.description: Big, fair, gentle, unmarried, keeps hens and the island's best garden; Galen Coombs's aunt. Walks out to the end of the Point every afternoon to look at the water. Not frightened; homesick for something she can't name.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To understand what happened to her, and to be told it was not her fault.

npcsInvolved.name: Galen Coombs, 38
npcsInvolved.role: The island's rum-runner; Peg Tolman's buyer
npcsInvolved.description: Dark, compact, handsome in a hard way, Navy tattoos, a gold tooth, a good wool coat over a fisherman's jersey. Runs Sculpin Cove, two fast boats and twenty young men. Generous, funny, ruthless, and secretly frightened of the bell, which nearly took his aunt.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Keep his business safe from the law and the island safe from the bell; he thinks a box of dynamite will do the second (see db-scenario-002).

npcsInvolved.name: Thankful Lunt, 80
npcsInvolved.role: Zeb Lunt's sister-in-law; keeper of the ballad
npcsInvolved.description: Very small and upright, a choir voice older than the new church, sharp eyes, a shawl and a cane. Lives with her daughter in the Harbor. Knows four verses of 'The Carrow Bell' and what the last one means.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the song, and not to be the one who says what it says.

npcsInvolved.name: Peleg Sprague, Kingsley Trask, Oren Pinkham and Mattie Grindle
npcsInvolved.description: Peleg, the grinning Sprague mechanic who rang in August; Kingsley, the young minister who stopped the ringing and bought the new bell; Oren, the keeper with two logbooks; Mattie, the Point Grindles' last daughter, who says the word 'shut'.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Each has their own; see their dmNotes.

rewards.money: Peg Tolman's buyer pays $1,800 for the whisky (Galen counts it out in tens on a herring barrel); Pearl Haverty's $50 balance from Verna, if she earns it, or not; Merrymeeting Life pays Len Garrity his week whatever happens. The island pays nobody, but a party that saved someone on Tuesday will find their bills at the Store marked paid, a mess of lobsters on the step every morning, and Verna's boarders' rent waived.
items: Zeb Lunt's ringing book, with the names on the flyleaf and, in the back, upside down, the last verse (CLUE F1 if found)
Imogen Lisle's cylinders of 'The Carrow Bell', verses one to three
A copy of the 1924 lighthouse log entries, in Oren's hand
Esther Thurlow's notebook, and Eliphalet Tibbetts's 1871 letter from the attic trunk
The Saint-Pierre letter from Verna's sugar tin, if taken
The key to the church tower, and the island's leave to ring the bell at every spring low

twists: If Dr. Thurlow goes down to the Point on Tuesday evening to see where his sister walked, he is the one called. The GM should let him: it is the most frightening thing in the scenario, and the party's first proof that the rules are fair and the danger is real. Make the player's choice of walking a pleasure, not a horror, for them; the horror is for everyone watching.

The seance tells the truth about Clyde Tibbetts in front of witnesses, and by Monday morning Galen Coombs has heard that a ghost said Clyde is alive. Galen goes to Verna. Whether the party protect her decides what she will tell them, and whether Galen trusts them.

Ellery Wyman cut the 14 to 20 October 1871 pages out of the board of health minute book himself, in September, after Jotham, when he read them for the first time. He burned them. He will deny it until db-scenario-003. What they said is in Oren's father's log and Orpha's Bible.

Len Garrity is right about Clyde. Let him be right, and let it matter: There's an Explanation works, the island's one fraud is exposed, and the other three drownings are left standing with no explanation at all.
dmTips: This scenario is about learning three rules in five days and using them on the sixth. Every core clue is found by anyone who looks in the right place; rolls add detail and speed, never gate the truth. If the party reach Tuesday morning without knowing Rule 3, have Peleg Sprague tell them, privately and miserably, what he did on 16 August.

Keep the tide visible. Mention it every scene: the harbor mud, the Bar dry or covered, the weed on the pilings. By Tuesday the players should be able to tell you the time of low water without looking.

Nothing attacks anyone in this scenario. The horror is a bell, a seance, footprints in the sea, and a friend standing up and walking away from you with a happy face. Resist adding a fight; the Drowned do not come ashore until the doors are opened in db-scenario-002.

The islanders are decent people carrying something. Ellery is grieving, the old men are frightened, Verna is desperate, Orpha is worn through. Play them as neighbors who want the strangers gone because they are ashamed, not because they are sinister.

The called is answering a name, nothing else. Describe the walk as joy, homecoming, a name called in a loved voice, every time, and never as a wish to die. If a player at the table is uncomfortable, cut away to the tower and the rope.

Peg Tolman's whisky, Len Garrity's fraud and Pearl Haverty's seance are the human comedy that keeps the horror from being monotonous; let them be funny. A bootlegger arguing with a minister about a bell full of rye is a good scene.

Budget an hour for Friday, two hours across Saturday to Monday, and an hour and a half for Tuesday. The ringing should come at the end of a session, and Orpha's warning about the lowest tide at the very end.
